 Cyberattack targets Optimizely, third-party software used by major websites
 The attack reportedly impacted nearly 200 websites, with malware designed to steal credit card information and cryptocurrency
 Pamela Osborne , Anchor/Reporter
 Published:  November 17, 2026 at 4:56 PM Tags:  Cyber Security What we know 
 A new cyberattack is raising concerns about the security risks tied to third-party software used to help run some of the world’s biggest websites.
 Optimizely — a company that provides tools used to power and manage websites for businesses and organizations — was targeted in an attack in which malicious code was injected into a software supply chain.
 Rhongho Jang, Assistant Professor of Computer Science at Wayne State University, said the attack highlights a broader challenge: as technology evolves quickly — including the use of artificial intelligence — defenses do not always keep pace with attackers’ ability to abuse new tools.
 A new cyberattack is raising concerns about the security risks tied to third-party software used to help run some of the world’s biggest websites. (Copyright 2026 by WDIV ClickOnDetroit - All rights reserved.) How the attack worked 
 Jang said the risk with third-party web tools is that everyday users may unknowingly rely on them simply by visiting a website.
 He explained that when a web browser loads a public site, it can also pull in software components from third-party providers.
 During that process, Jang said, attackers can inject malicious code into the third-party delivery pipeline — potentially spreading it to multiple sites at once.
 What the malware was designed to do 
 According to Reuters, the malware in this incident was designed to skim credit card payments and steal cryptocurrency.
 Jang said what data is at risk can depend on what site a person is visiting.
 “If you’re working on a bank website, it will steal your account information,” Jang said, adding that the impact can vary based on the targeted site.
 How widespread was it? 
 Nearly 200 websites were reportedly impacted, and Apple users faced an additional exploit attempt designed to gain higher privileges on iPhones — potentially seeking access to information such as photos or other permissions commonly granted to apps.
 It is not clear how successful those exploit attempts were.
 Optimizely response 
 Optimizely said it has addressed the issue.
 In a statement, the company said: “We’ve fixed the vulnerability and removed the injected code from affected projects. We’ve also taken steps to secure affected user accounts and put additional protections in place to prevent unauthorized code from being delivered.”
 What you can do 
 Jang said there often isn’t much consumers can do to prevent this kind of third-party supply-chain attack in advance.
 However, he said once companies identify and patch these issues, they are less likely to happen again in the same way.
 Jang also said AI could help speed up detection and response in coming years — shifting the cycle from “catch-up” to more long-term stability.
